comparator.sourceNotes: Checked 2026-11-13. The verified subset is now150EC: the original120EC first-two-year prescribed/restricted-choice inventory plus30EC genuine elective space, independently established by the applicable current faculty OER. The faculty text expressly lists History under its scope and is jointly applicable with the OSO. Articles3.1.1/3.2.1 establish150required+30openEC;3.2.3–3.2.6 govern level, board approval and non-overlap, with recognised30EC Leiden/Delft/Erasmus minors exempt from separate approval and Honours excluded. History OSO3.2.9 excludes overlapping AmericanHistory and Medieval/EarlyModern minor tracks. AppendixB requires supervised research, engagement with primary material, seminar support, normally at least10EC and a second reader; exact programme allocation and any deviation belong in the guide. Do not count that minimum as an exact thesis component. The original20 component identities/weights and illustrated annual choices remain unchanged. Both first-year research seminars are accepted for BA2 entry; study-advice and individual conditions apply. OSO2.2 removes formal routes for2025+ entrants and AppendixF defers BA3 transition to2027–2028. Current BA-GES identifies2026–2027 as the last old-style third year; forward2271 returns the same current record. The public2526 diagram is historical, not the source of the newly confirmed30EC. The remaining30requiredEC, exact revised final-work/seminar allocation and programme progression remain unverified. Preserve all29interest/42course findings and three feasible provisional24-course proposals; retired-route rationales and alignments remain historical. GOSHIST312 uses only its current name/description, not the archived Walcheren outline. Primary source is the human-readable official History page. No app or Excel changes. Stage 2 assesses only the confirmed first-two-year academic core, retaining genuine 30-EC open study separately. No retired formal route, old third-year thesis/entry rule, future offering or complete degree equivalence is claimed.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: History across ancient, medieval, early-modern and modern periods, with European, Dutch and global perspectives
Historical explanation of social, cultural, economic and political change and its relevance to current society
Power, inequality, migration, war, states and international connections in historical development
Original sources, historiography, archival and material evidence, historical methods and academic writing
Economic and social history and the interaction of institutions, markets, social groups and political change
Historical research seminars, evidence-based debate and communication of interpretations within the confirmed first-two-year core; revised final work excluded
adjacent: Politics, international relations, empire, war and conflict in historical perspective
Social and economic history, migration and inequality
Cultural history, heritage, memory, representation and public uses of the past
questions: How do long-term historical developments explain present political, economic, social and cultural conditions?
How can original sources, material evidence and competing interpretations be analysed critically?
How have power, empire, conflict, migration and inequality shaped Europe and the wider world?

trace: establishes microeconomic and macroeconomic concepts for interpreting historical economic change
examines long-run growth, crises, trade and fiscal and monetary policy in the international economy

Develops microeconomic models of choice, market power, uncertainty, externalities and allocation, with critical evaluation of economic research. These tools support interpreting economic institutions and distribution, without promising a history-of-economic-thought sequence.
analyses taxation, public spending, redistribution, political economy, efficiency and inequality
provides quantitative tools for causal and predictive analysis of economic and social data
uses experiments and behavioural theory to study decision-making and economic conduct
teaches research design, operationalisation, sampling and descriptive and inferential statistics
places legal systems and institutions in social, historical and normative context
provides a chronological survey of modern political, economic and cultural history from 1815
uses gender and intersectional perspectives to study lives, identities, activism and historical storytelling
compares empires, imperial power and theories of their rise, rule and decline across world history
traces warfare, technology, state power and conflict from antiquity to the present
studies Indigenous histories, forced assimilation, resistance, memory and cultural regeneration

Current Researching the American Century develops research questions, critical source engagement, methodological rigour and a substantial historical paper. No archived Walcheren topic, guaranteed archival technique or15EC independent-thesis equivalence is assumed.
traces human rights through positive law, historical development and philosophical argument
examines the historical evolution, institutions and doctrines of international law and armed conflict
compares constitutional institutions, state power, rights and administrative authority
examines European integration, EU institutions and the interaction of European and national legal orders
places influential theories of society, authority and justice in their historical settings
compares political systems, democratisation, institutions, parties and contemporary political change
uses historical and contemporary cases to test theories of international relations and geopolitics
analyses EU institutions, decision-making, public authority and competing state and non-state interests
integrates history, sociology, politics and law in the study of conflict, violence and peacebuilding
introduces social theory and institutions in socio-historical and global context
teaches qualitative design, interpretation, reflexivity, data collection and dissemination
examines modernity, imperialism, colonial responses and the development of social theory
develops advanced global social theory around civil society, solidarity, trust and institutional repair
Classical rhetorical history, argument evaluation, written debate and public speech support historical argument and explanation. Its applied public project does not guarantee a historical subject.
surveys Western art from the Renaissance to the present and teaches visual and historiographical analysis
uses material culture and archaeology to compare ancient societies, identities and production
studies African art, heritage, colonial appropriation, cultural meaning and repatriation
places Renaissance Italy in the connected cultural history of the global Mediterranean
examines museums, exhibitions and curatorial practices as makers of modern public memory

Studies historiography and interpretive methods of art history from the sixteenth century onward through key scholarly texts. This is specific visual-cultural historiography, not a general archival-research course.
connects past and present through stories of race, power, erasure, resistance and public memory
traces documentary history and develops critical and practical analysis of non-fiction representation
R-based text, tabular and geospatial-data analysis provides concrete tools for digital historical-source inquiry; it is not QGIS training or a guaranteed historical project.
Studies early Greek community and democracy through its material culture, adding a concrete ancient historical case; absent detailed methods remain unasserted.
Uses primary texts and archaeological evidence to investigate Athenian citizenship, exclusions, religion and democratic crises through historical research and grounded simulation.
Investigates historical media objects, manuscript/print relations and technological materiality through artifact and source analysis, connecting historical evidence to communication and memory.

candidates.label: Social and economic history, migration and inequality

selection.assessment: Closest material-cultural history, politics/conflict, then social/economic inquiry each pass independently at the limited first-two-year core scope. All retain substantive historical/source research and have different sustained adjacent curricula. Three is the maximum; no additional career- or example-generated slot.

alternatives.label: History, society & cultural memory
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines substantive historical inquiry with material culture, heritage, media and cultural memory. The label does not claim a full disciplinary History major or a Leiden formal route.
alternatives.concept: Study historical change through the full UCR History sequence, source criticism and research, alongside archaeology, material and visual culture, media history, historiography and cultural memory. Ancient Greek, imperial, modern and Indigenous inquiries provide concrete historical cases, with digital data methods supporting source-based work.
progression: 24 unique courses/180 EC, four per term, Year-1 PPD and at least six advanced; real offerings and earlier formal prerequisites verified. Introductions precede advanced historical inquiry where possible. No extra hard prerequisite inferred.

alternatives.label: History, politics & conflict
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines substantive historical inquiry with politics, institutions, law and conflict. The label does not claim a full disciplinary History major or a Leiden formal route.
alternatives.concept: Combine the full UCR History sequence with sustained study of political institutions, international order, law, rights and conflict. Historical source inquiry and contemporary institutional/legal analysis provide different methods for examining power and political change.
progression: 24 unique courses/180 EC, four per term, Year-1 PPD and at least six advanced; real offerings and earlier formal prerequisites verified. Introductions precede advanced historical inquiry where possible. No extra hard prerequisite inferred.
alternatives.distinctness: Retains historical source inquiry while replacing the closest material/visual/archaeological and media concentration with sustained law, comparative politics, international relations, institutions and conflict. These changes implement political-development interest 13343 rather than a new formal History route.

alternatives.label: History, inequality & political economy
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines substantive historical inquiry with sociology, economic explanation and empirical political economy. The label does not claim a full disciplinary History major or a Leiden formal route.
alternatives.concept: Combine the full UCR History sequence with economics, sociology, institutions and empirical methods to examine social change, inequality and political economy. Renaissance Mediterranean exchange adds a concrete early-modern cultural/economic connection; economic models complement rather than replace historical explanation.
progression: 24 unique courses/180 EC, four per term, Year-1 PPD and at least six advanced; real offerings and earlier formal prerequisites verified. Introductions precede advanced historical inquiry where possible. No extra hard prerequisite inferred.
alternatives.distinctness: Retains historical source inquiry while replacing the closest material/media focus and the second program's legal/conflict focus with economics, sociology, inequality and empirical political economy. New Renaissance exchange and data methods strengthen concrete historical and analytical inquiry.

blocks: Both investigate modern political, social and cultural change from the nineteenth century onward. Leiden also includes a substantial early-modern European survey and historical labs.

Both develop historical inquiry through source interpretation, research and presentation. UCR uses gendered and oral-history cases; Leiden introduces an assigned historical theme, literature work and a specified paper sequence. This is a partial research-function relationship, not identical subjects or assessment.

Comparative imperial history directly investigates cross-regional power, institutions, exchange and historical connection. Leiden additionally teaches the broader historiography and scale-sensitive methods of global history.

Both develop a historical question, critical engagement with sources and a substantial research paper. UCR studies American-century inquiry; Leiden advances its own research-seminar sequence. No revised final-thesis equivalence is implied.
Material culture, heritage and historical representation

World Archaeology studies ancient societies through material culture, providing a substantive ancient-past relationship. Leiden offers a dedicated historical survey with its own chronology and textual labs.

Both investigate citizenship, political participation and exclusion historically. UCR concentrates on ancient Athens through primary texts and material evidence; Leiden follows citizenship and subjecthood from antiquity to the present.
Both examine disciplinary historiography and interpretation through scholarly arguments. UCR focuses on art history; Leiden studies general historical theory and historiographical traditions.

Both teach practical handling and analysis of data with spatial applications. UCR uses R and general tabular/text/geospatial workflows; Leiden teaches QGIS mapping of historical primary-source datasets. The tools, domain assignments and scope differ.
External core without a separately paired UCR course
The History courses supply historical inquiry, but no separately allocated course reproduces this dedicated introduction to historical science.
No selected course provides a dedicated Dutch-history survey.
Empires, warfare and archaeology include medieval cases, but no selected course supplies the dedicated medieval-history survey.
World/imperial and material histories contribute, but the paired Empires course is counted once; no separate course reproduces this four-region survey and historical labs.
The third UCR program adds economic/social analysis; these courses do not reproduce this long-run European/Dutch historical survey and primary-source labs.
Digital-data and historical-media study contribute elsewhere, but no separately allocated selected course reproduces the full humanities-in-a-digital-world module.
Historical and art-historical interpretation do not replace a dedicated philosophy-of-science module.
Modern History includes Russian/Soviet developments, but no separately allocated selected course provides this Russia-focused historical lecture.
No selected course supplies the specific African medical, climate and environmental-history seminar. African art/heritage is a different subject.
No selected course teaches papyrological text sources specifically. Leiden uses translated texts and requires no Greek, Latin or Egyptian language here.
No selected course provides this Caribbean historical lecture. Indigenous North American inquiry has different regional and source objects.
Historical source research and imperial/warfare study are present, but no selected course supplies the specific Spanish Philip II research seminar.
Genuine 30-EC open study is preserved without an assumed subject or one-course equivalence. Level, approval and non-overlap restrictions apply.

notes.text: This comparison assesses the confirmed first-two-year History core. The table also preserves 30 EC of genuine open study without assigning its contents. The remaining 30 required EC, exact revised final research and full progression are excluded. UCR provides sustained historical inquiry with different interdisciplinary emphases; dedicated medieval/Dutch surveys, specialist regional seminars and some source methods remain gaps. No full History-major or thesis equivalence is claimed.

audience.programmeDescription: Leiden History studies political, social, economic and cultural change from antiquity to the present, with attention to Europe and its connections with the world. Source criticism, historical research and written and oral argument are central. The revised first two years include digital humanities and a sequence of research seminars.
audience.comparisonExplanation: This qualified academic-core comparison relates Leiden’s confirmed first two years to three UCR programs with sustained historical study and different material-cultural, political or socioeconomic emphases. The 30 EC of genuine open study is retained without assumed contents. The remaining 30 required EC, revised final research and full progression are excluded. Dedicated medieval and Dutch surveys, specialist regional seminars and some source methods remain differences.

curriculum.limitation: Verified subset: 150 of 180 EC. This includes 60 EC of required first-year study, 60 EC of second-year required study and restricted choices, and 30 EC of elective space. The illustrated choices reflect the current annual menu and do not guarantee future offerings. Formal routes do not apply to entrants from 2025 onward. The remaining 30 required EC and their programme-specific final research and progression rules await confirmation. Both first-year research seminars must be passed before second-year research seminars; the usual study-advice threshold is 45 EC with at least one first-year research seminar passed. Individual course conditions also apply. Electives must meet level, approval and non-overlap rules.

componentNotes.y2-5532vpsy: Restricted 5 EC sources-and-methods choice. Entry requires Ancient History and the study-advice norm. Assessment includes assignments, a final paper and an oral presentation. No selected course teaches papyrological text sources specifically. Leiden uses translated texts and requires no Greek, Latin or Egyptian language here.
componentNotes.y2-5772ibm02y: Restricted 5 EC sources-and-methods choice, open to BA History students. Weekly assignments and a take-home examination each contribute half the grade.
componentNotes.y2-5732v013y: Restricted 10 EC autumn research seminar. The study-advice norm and both first-year research seminars must be passed; assessment includes a substantial research paper, participation and individual/group presentations. No selected course supplies the specific African medical, climate and environmental-history seminar. African art/heritage is a different subject.
componentNotes.y2-5772iaw62y: Restricted 10 EC spring research seminar. The study-advice norm and both first-year research seminars must be passed. The paper must pass; presentations, group work and participation also contribute. Historical source research and imperial/warfare study are present, but no selected course supplies the specific Spanish Philip II research seminar.
componentNotes.open-elective-space: 30 EC for appropriate-level elective study or a minor. Examination-board approval is required except for recognised 30 EC minors at Leiden, Delft or Erasmus. Courses must not overlap with required study, and Honours courses cannot count. History also excludes overlapping American History and Medieval/Early Modern History minor tracks. No particular elective subjects or semester split are assumed.

acceptance.claim: The confirmed 120-EC historical core supports meaningful UCR programs combining sustained historical and source-based inquiry with material culture/memory, political institutions/conflict, or social and economic explanation. Genuine 30-EC open study is retained separately. This is not a complete History-major or final-year comparison; known chronological, regional and specialist-method gaps remain.
acceptance.targetContext: Ordinary Leiden BA History 56034/1001O5816, revised 2026–2027 first-two-year inventory and neutral annual choices; no retired formal route or future offering/access guarantee.
acceptance.challengeMethod: Separately identified same-AI source-first final pass against actual official/UCR content and exact finished inputs; no independent human or separate-agent endorsement.

uncertainties.fact: Revised third-year required 30 EC, precise final-work/seminar allocation and full programme progression remain unpublished or unreconciled. The outgoing 15-EC thesis and formal-route requirements cannot establish them.

adverseResolutions.resolution: Later required study deepens a particular period, source language/technique, archival investigation or independent thesis formation.
adverseResolutions.effectOnClaim: Those final-year subjects, access conditions and culmination could materially change a full-degree comparison and are excluded. The already confirmed historical surveys, labs and research-seminar core still has sustained actual UCR historical/source inquiry. Known specialist gaps remain visible; no assumed project fills them.

adverseResolutions.resolution: Later required study emphasizes broad cultural, political, socioeconomic or digital historical inquiry and different research organization.
adverseResolutions.effectOnClaim: Do not import a guessed unit or credit. The three narrower core responses remain supported by current historical content and distinct taught methods; neither final-year equivalence nor a complete entrant pathway follows.

uncertainties.fact: Current restricted-choice names and some module entry wording are annual examples; no retired formal route or future-cohort eligibility is certified. Full fresh programme-specific OSO body was inaccessible; exact same-year 13 November findings retained.

adverseResolutions.resolution: A new annual menu replaces individual illustrated seminars or adopted rules add preparation/permission requirements for future students.
adverseResolutions.effectOnClaim: The dated core illustration remains accurately limited and contains no future offering promise or access waiver. Reassess material new core evidence when separately authorized. Generic History identity, historical source/research functions and current methods are not contingent on an invented retired route.
